analytic.title: Research on Real-Time Linux Task Scheduling Algorithm for Multiprocessors Based on Particle Swarm Optimisation

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Schedulability analysis in real-time operating systems is one of the hot research topics in the field. While Linux has become the preferred choice for industrial systems due to its excellent portability, it cannot meet the hard realtime requirements of specific industrial environments as a timesharing operating system. To address this issue, we introduce the Real-Time Application Interface (RTAI) 5.2 real-time operating system kernel patch and combine it with Linux 4.4.176 to form the RTAI-Linux dual-core real-time system. Building upon this foundation, we proposes a Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm based on Earliest Deadline First (PSO-EDF) to improve task scheduling in real-time Linux multiprocessor environments. This method introduces a metric for evaluating processor utilization, when a new task arrives, it considers the allocation of free processor resources. Compared with the original method EDF, PSO-EDF provides a broader search space with better global characteristics. The algorithm finds the globally optimal scheduling scheme through iteration, which effectively improves the processor resource utilisation and alleviates the task deadline missing problem encountered in the original method to a certain extent, thus improving the real-time task completion rate. Through extensive simulation experiments, the PSO-EDF scheduling algorithm proves that the scheduling model can further improve the real-time performance of the RTAI-Linux system compared with the classical EDF algorithm.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: As computer technology and integrated circuits have advanced, embedded systems have been widely applied in various industries. Due to its excellent scalability and portability, the Linux operating system has become the preferred choice for embedded systems. However, linux as a time-sharing system, it has certain limitations when applied in industrial production environments with higher real-time requirements, such as the automotive and aerospace industries [1], [6]. In order to meet the needs of real-time tasks, improving Linux into a real-time operating system is a mainstream solution. In this paper, we will use RTAI 5.2 real-time kernel patch and linux 4.4.176 to form a dual-kernel real-time Linux operating system. But the simple use of RTAI does not strictly realtime processing of real-time tasks, the real-time nature of the system still has room for improvement [2].

Optimising the scheduling model in the operating system can improve the real-time performance of the system to a certain extent. The classical scheduling algorithms of Linux include Earliest Deadline First (EDF), First In First Out (FIFO) and Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). As the primary scheduling policy in the Linux system, EDF demonstrates promising scheduling performance. However, it still faces sev-eral challenges and issues [3]. EDF assigns the highest priority to the task with the earliest deadline. However, this scheduling approach may not always find the global optimal solution. If a task fails to complete within its deadline due to incomplete utilization of processor resources or hardware-related factors, it can trigger a "domino effect", causing subsequent tasks to miss their deadlines as well. Previous work investigated an EDF scheduling approach for arbitrary sequences [4] To address this issue, this paper proposes a Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm based on Earliest Deadline First (PSO-EDF) to optimize the resource allocation problem of multiprocessor tasks in real-time Linux systems. In the improved algorithm, we introduced a metric to evaluate processor resource utilization. We incorporated the number of tasks completed within their deadlines and the processor resource utilization into the objective function as evaluation criteria for the scheduling performance. By adopting this approach, we establish a more reasonable resource allocation strategy for processors, which helps mitigate the potential occurrence of the "domino effect" to some extent. By adjusting the speed and position update strategy of particles, it can adapt to the changing requirements of real-time tasks and provide dynamic task scheduling and resource allocation strategies, thus improving the adaptability and flexibility of real-time task scheduling in RTAI-Linux. By enhancing the real-time task scheduling model based on the RTAI-Linux operating system, it is possible to address the issue of task deadline misses on multiple processors to a certain extent. Simultaneously, the processor utilization can be improved, leading to a substantial enhancement of the real-time performance of the Linux system. This approach aligns with the real-time requirements of industrial production environments, making it well-suited for such applications.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Enhancing the real-time Linux system is an important research content, real-time systems in the schedulable analysis can not be ignored, a good scheduling algorithm for improving the performance of the multiprocessor system has an important significance [5]. Linux systems have real-time patches such as RTAI, PREEMPT-RT, and Xenomai. Systems employing the RTAI interface framework demonstrate better performance in specific scenarios. For scheduling approaches in real-time operating systems, recent research has shown that performing internal scheduling analyses has not been as widely [7].

EDF, as an inherent dynamic task scheduling algorithm in Linux, is one of the mainstream scheduling algorithms. It has been widely applied on single processors with mature systems. However, there may be some challenges when transplanting the EDF scheduling concept to multiple processors. In previous work, the researchers proposed one criticality one partition (OCOP) method to fully utilise processor. resources [8]. In previous work, a priority-driven scheduling algorithm based on EDF has been proposed, which improves the performance of EDF in multiprocessor systems. However, the allocation of processor resources and metrics are manually customised and are not adaptive. [9]. Additionally, in previous research, there were investigations regarding two multi-processor-based Nested Partition Earliest Deadline First (NP-EDF) algorithms for schedulability tests, which enhanced scheduling performance [10].

Moreover, researchers proposed a new algorithm based on the PSO algorithm, aiming to achieve the maximum number of executions in the shortest time possible [11]. Previously, researchers introduced an Improved Particle Swarm Optimization (IPSO) algorithm to discretize the Particle Swarm Optimization representation. This approach enabled its application to multi-processor scheduling problems while combining it with a genetic algorithm [12]. By employing a method that introduces task importance weights and combines the idea of a greedy algorithm for single-processor resource allocation enhancement, it is possible to address the potential "domino effect" issue of EDF on a single processor. However, this approach cannot be extended to multi-processor task scheduling [13], [14]. The researchers present an energy-efficient task partitioning approach for asymmetric multiprocessor platforms that utilises improved particle swarm optimisation methods to minimise energy consumption and ensure timely task execution [15].

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND ALGORITHM DESCRIPTION
div.p: A. RTAI-Linux RTAI defines a set of Real-Time Hardware Abstraction Layer (RTHAL) on Linux, which gathers all the necessary pointers to Linux internal data and functions into an RTHAL structure. This structure is then used to intercept Linux hardware operations, redirecting them to replace the original functions. This approach minimally alters the Linux kernel, overcoming the issue of RT-Linux making excessive changes to the source kernel. RTAI is a preemptive kernel that incorporates real-time Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) features, including real-time interrupt response. The RTAI-Linux dual kernel system offers distinct advantages: real-time tasks are executed using RTAI, while non-real-time and refinementneeded tasks utilize the Linux kernel. Overall, the integration of RTAI into Linux through RTHAL provides a more efficient and streamlined approach to real-time operations, optimizing the performance of both real-time and non-real-time tasks within a single system.

div.head: B. Particle Swarm Optimization
div.p: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a population intelligence algorithm inspired by the behaviour of a flock of birds or a school of fish. PSO finds the optimal solution by simulating the movement of particles in the search space. It does this by maintaining the position and velocity of each particle and guiding the movement of the particles with information about the individual optimum and the global optimum. In particle swarm algorithm, each particle represents a potential solution with position and velocity. The particle updates its velocity and position according to its own historical optimal position (individual optimal) and the historical optimal position of the whole group (global optimal). Through continuous iteration, the swarm of particles gradually clusters around the optimal solution in the search space. In the particle swarm algorithm, each particle represents a potential solution and has a position and velocity. The particles update their velocities and positions according to their own historical optimal positions (individual optimal) and the historical optimal positions of the whole swarm (global optimal). Through continuous iteration, the particle swarm gradually gathers near the optimal solution in the search space. div.head: C. Earliest Deadline First
div.p: Earliest Deadline First (EDF) is the prioritisation of tasks based on their start deadline. The earlier the deadline, the higher the priority. The algorithm requires that a real-time task-ready queue be maintained in the system, which is sorted according to the early or late deadline of each task, the task with the earliest deadline is at the top of the queue. The scheduler always selects the first task in the ready queue when selecting a task, allocates a processor for it, and puts it into operation. The earliest deadline first algorithm can be used in both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling methods. Computational tasks with explicit time constraints are called real-time tasks, and the tasks are further classified into stochastic real-time tasks and periodic real-time tasks.

div.head: A. Comparing EDF and PSO-EDF
div.p: The problems of the EDF scheduling algorithm described above can affect the real-time performance of the Linux system, in order to solve this problem, we propose the model PSO-EDF which applies PSO to improve the EDF scheduling algorithm. The optimal scheduling scheme is selected by designing the fitness function instead of scheduling by the deadline of the task only. Suppose there are four tasks T 1 , T 2 , T 3 , T 4 , two processors P 1 , P 2 , M is the task execution time and N is the deadline for the task. where the tasks T 1 : M = 2, N = 4; T 2 : M = 3, N = 5; T 3 : M = 4, N = 7; T 4 : M = 5, N = 7. We use EDF and PSO-EDF scheduling models respectively, and we find that T 4 will be executed on P 2 due to its later priority, which leads to missing the deadline of the task, relatively speaking, P 1 is free for 1 time slice, and when promoted to a large number of tasks, this situation will lead to problems such as uneven resource allocation, and it becomes even more troublesome in a heterogeneous multiprocessor system. When we used the PSO-EDF scheduling scheme, we make full use of the processor free time by adding the processor resource utilisation to the fitness function, as seen in the fact that we put T 4 into P 1 for execution, so that each task completes its own scheduling before the deadline. The PSO-EDF model may have different scheduling results each time, but usually the algorithm is able to gradually improve the scheduling order and resource allocation of tasks through the process of searching for the optimal solution in order to satisfy the deadline requirements of realtime tasks and improve the overall real-time performance of the system.

However, this process can lead to a many-toone mapping relationship, resulting in numerous invalid and redundant scheduling solutions. This increases the size of the particle population, reducing the efficiency of task scheduling. The initialization step is critical to provide a diverse initial solution set for the particles, which is the starting point for the optimization process in PSO-EDF. Firstly, we need to initialize the velocity and position of the particle swarm. In the algorithm, each particle represents a potential scheduling solution. We define an n×m matrix X to describe the position information of the particles and an n × n matrix V to describe the velocity information of the particles.

where n represents the number of real-time tasks, m represents the number of processors, the elements of the matrix X represent the position of each particle in solution space, corresponding to the situation where the tasks in the scheduling problem are located in the processor. The constraint x ij means that a task can only be executed on one processor at a time.

The random position of the matrix means that tasks are randomly assigned to processors. The velocity is defined as the basic exchange sequence required for a particle to transition from its current position to the target state. It is represented by a matrix as follows,

where the elements of the matrix V represent the speed of each particle in the optimization process. The velocity constraint implies that in the velocity matrix, elements v ij and v ji cannot both be equal to 1 simultaneously. This constraint is applied to avoid the occurrence of ineffective and redundant swap operations during a single update process. We determine the initial velocity range based on the number of processors and tasks. For example, we may use random values in [-1, 1] or in [-2, 2]. The particle's velocity represents the extent of changes in the task scheduling solution, specifically indicating the frequency of task switching between processors. In this context, a positive velocity value suggests that tasks are frequently being switched between processors, while a negative velocity value indicates a lower frequency of task switching. By initializing the velocity with random values within the specified range, the algorithm allows the particles to explore different solution spaces and find better task scheduling schemes that optimize the overall performance of the system. Next, we will design the fitness function for the particles. The fitness function, also known as the objective function, represents the goal to be optimized. It is defined to evaluate the performance of the particles. Our designed fitness function calculates a fitness value based on the task deadlines and resource allocation for each particle. This fitness value is used to measure the quality of the particle's solution, indicating how well it performs in terms of meeting task deadlines and efficiently allocating resources. By using this fitness function, the PSO-EDF aims to find the optimal scheduling solution that maximizes the fitness value, leading to improved task completion rates and enhanced utilization of processor resources in the multi-processor task scheduling problem. The fitness function is designed as follows,
div.formula: f s(T i ) = α( s n ) + β ( t 1 T 1 + t 2 T 2 + • • • + t n T n )/n(10)
div.p: where f s(T i ) represents the fitness function for task T i , encompassing two components: the number of tasks that meet the deadline requirements and the processor resource utilization.

In this context, s signifies the count of tasks that satisfy the deadline requirements, and n denotes the total number of tasks in the system. The weight coefficient α, β is introduced to balance the relative importance of these two indicators within the fitness function, enabling effective optimization. Furthermore, t 1 , t 2 , . . . , t n represent the execution times of tasks on each processor, while T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T n denote the total time available on each processor for task execution. Subsequently, we need to design the update formulas for particle velocity and position. Since the particle's position is no longer a continuous vector, and its velocity and position cannot be updated as previously shown in Equation 5, we have adopted a special encoding approach based on the work proposed by other researchers [15]. Finally, we return the solution corresponding to the global best position as the optimized result. To achieve the maximum value of the fitness function, we must decode the particle into a feasible scheduling scheme. We count the elements with a value of 1 in each row of the particle position matrix, which provides us with the task allocation vector for each processor. By sorting the task allocation vector based on task priority rules, we obtain a feasible task execution sequence. Ultimately, based on the particle position encoding of the global best solution, we perform the corresponding scheduling work on each processor.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS
div.p: There are two important metrics that affect the real-time performance of a real-time operating system, task switching time and interrupt response timeinterrupt. Response Time = Longest Interruption Time + Time to Protect CPU Internal Register + Execution Time of Interrupt Service Function + Start Execute the first instruction time of the interrupt service routine (ISR).Table 1 shows typical performance metrics for several real-time systems. We can see that Preempt RT has an average context switching time of 0.80 and an RTAI of 0.49, while in terms of interrupt response it is 12.4 vs 4.3.

In this paper, with reference to the RTAI-Linux kernel structure, the model of the system task control block is modified and multiple random tasks are generated, where the number of experimentally generated tasks T i ∈ (4, 5, • • • , 64) to simulate execution on two processors. The execution time of the tasks is randomly generated within [1,50], and the weight size of the fitness function is weighted 0.7 and 0.3, respectively, and these randomly generated tasks are scheduled using the PSO-EDF and EDF algorithms, respectively, and by comparing the as-of-time of the task it is possible to determine whether the deadline is missed. It should be noted that, due to the different selection of the execution time of the test task and the deadline time, the may lead to different results for different experiments, the closer the execution time is to the deadline may lead to a higher number of missed tasks, and the results of each scheduling of this model may be different, but usually, it is able to go through the process of searching for the optimal solution in order to satisfy the deadline requirements of real-time tasks. The results of the experiments carried out iteratively with this algorithm are shown in Fig4. From the experimental results, the number of tasks with the number of tasks is 4, the number of tasks with missed deadlines for EDF and PSO-EDF tasks are 1 and 0; as the number of tasks increases, the missed rate of the EDF algorithm tasks is almost 0.8, while the PSO-EDF tasks have a missed rate of 0.7, and relative to the traditional scheduling algorithms our algorithm is able to reduce the number of tasks by 10% of the task miss rate. This shows that both scheduling models are able to me into the angle of the task better under lower load, but as the number of tasks increases, both algorithms will have the number of missed tasks to a certain extent, which is not a very huge improvement compared to the EDF algorithm, but achieves the optimisation purpose. Moreover, for RT-Linux our algorithm can effectively improve the system realtime performance. In conclusion, our enhanced real-time task scheduling model provides a robust solution to the challenges of multiprocessor environments, ensuring timely execution of tasks while maximising processor resource utilisation.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In order to improve the real-time performance of linux system, we use RTAI real-time kernel to form a dual-kernel real-time linux, and based on this, we propose PSO-EDF algorithm based on EDF algorithm to make full use of processor resources. The novelty and main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We use RTAI5.2 and Linux4.4.176 to form a dual-kernel Linux system, which improves the real-time performance of the Linux system; 2. We design the PSO-EDF algorithm, which improves the problem that the processor resources are not fully utilised in the scheduling of the multiprocessor real-time linux, which leads to the task missing the deadline; 3. The practical contribution of this paper is that it can reduce the error rate of real-time tasks to a certain extent, so as to improve the stability and safety of real-time systems, which has a good application prospect in industrial production environments, embedded systems, and other computing environments, and provides a certain reference value for research in related fields.
